self_description.q: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop is a collaboration between Google's PAIR and Magenta teams, and 13 professional writers from a diverse set of creative writing backgrounds.

aim.q: Together we explore the limits of co-writing with LaMDA and foster an honest and earnest conversation about the rapidly changing relationship between technology and creativity.

writers_notice.q: The writers featured here have used Wordcraft along with their own creative vision and have not authored these stories under any sort of explicit guidance or instruction.

endorse.q: Google does not endorse the content of any of the stories contained on this website.

tool.q: Wordcraft is a tool built by researchers at Google PAIR for writing stories with AI. The application is powered by LaMDA

cohort.q: The workshop cohort consisted of 13 professional writers, who were given 8 weeks to use Wordcraft.

writers_world.q: we brought together 13 professional English-language writers from around the world to use Wordcraft to write stories

no_instruction.q: We explicitly didn't give writers any instructions regarding how they should use the tool or how much of their final story text should be directly generated by Wordcraft.

conducted.q: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop was conducted by Andy Coenen and Ann Yuan, research engineers on the PAIR team, Daphne Ippolito, a research scientist working with Magenta , and Sehmon Burnam, a product manager at Magenta .

paper_title.q: Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers

commissioned.q: we commissioned 13 professional, published writers from a diverse set of creative writing backgrounds to craft stories using Wordcraft

voice_finding.q: NLG technologies struggle to preserve style and authorial voice, and they lack deep understanding of story contents.

initials.q: We choose to refer to each participant by their initials (see Table 2) rather than anonymizing them because each writer's perspective is best understood within the context of their background and prior published work.

story_length.q: Participants were asked to write a story of 1,000-1,500 words using Wordcraft.

interviews.q: We also conducted two 45 minute interviews with each participant

consent.q: Participants consented to their stories being published in a digital literary magazine of human-AI collaborative stories, and to the use of their feedback in the journals and interviews in this whitepaper. Participants were compensated for participating in the study.

coding.q: Two authors of this paper coded the participants’ journals as well as the authors’ notes from the two interviews.

codes.q: Our high-level code set included 10 codes

generated_share.q: Several participants took the workshop as a challenge to produce a story that was largely formed around generated text (AP, DH, JM, MT, AW).

authored_share.q: the bulk of the story text was written by the authors themselves (KL, WT, NG).

siloed.q: some participants siloed out specific sections of their stories to which generated text could be included without the author needing to cede too much creative control to Wordcraft (RS).

origin_concern.q: professional writers face reputational harm if their work is found to have plagiarized, especially if the copied material came from smaller, more obscure writers.

rain_man.q: I finally settled on Rain Man

limit_design.q: Wordcraft was designed by engineers at Google with limited feedback from professional writers during its development.

limit_disambiguate.q: it is not easily possible to disambiguate weaknesses stemming from Wordcraft’s interface and implementation from inherent limitations of the underlying language model model backing Wordcraft.

limit_untested.q: but this study does not test this hypothesis.

limit_sample.q: our study was very small with only 13 participants, a sample that was biased toward people with pre-existing opinions on the role of AI in creative writing.

self_description.q: The ORCID ( / ˈ ɔːr k ɪ d / ⓘ ; Open Researcher and Contributor ID ) is a nonproprietary persistent identifier , in the form of an alphanumeric code, to uniquely identify authors and contributors of scholarly communication .

name_problem.q: This addresses the problem that a particular author's contributions to the scientific literature or humanities publications can be hard to recognize, as most personal names are not unique, they can change ( such as with marriage ), have cultural differences in name order, contain inconsistent use of first-name abbreviations and employ different writing systems .

self_description.q: The Virtual International Authority File ( VIAF ) is an international authority file . It is a joint project of several national libraries, operated by the Online Computer Library Center (OCLC).

link_not_build.q: After several failed attempts to develop a unique joint authority file, the new idea was to link existing national authorities.

initiated.q: The project was initiated by the American Library of Congress (LC), the German National Library (DNB), and the OCLC in April 1998 as a proof-of-concept that authority records can be linked.

oclc_service.q: The project transitioned to being a service of OCLC on 4 April 2012.

aim.q: The aim is to link the national authority files (such as the German Integrated Authority File ) to a single virtual authority file. In this file, identical records from the different data sets are linked together.

record.q: A VIAF record receives a standard data number, contains the primary "see" and "see also" records from the original documents, and refers to the original authority records.

access.q: The data is made available online and is available for research and, data exchange and sharing. Reciprocal updating uses the Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting (OAI-PMH) protocol.

wikidata.q: The file numbers are also being added to Wikipedia biographical articles and are incorporated into Wikidata .

borgman.q: Christine L. Borgman groups VIAF with the International Standard Name Identifier and ORCID systems, describing all three as "loosely coordinated efforts to standardize name forms".

libraries_led.q: She notes that VIAF, unlike the other two systems, is led by libraries, as opposed to individual authors or creators.

clusters.q: VIAF's clustering algorithm is run every month. As more data are added from participating libraries, clusters of authority records may coalesce or split, leading to some fluctuation in the VIAF identifier of certain authority records.

ubuweb.record_object: avant-garde materials: founded as a repository for visual, concrete and later sound poetry, and since then 'all forms of the avant-garde and beyond'; out-of-print, hard-to-find and obscure works transferred digitally to the web; Wikipedia (third party) adds film, music, early internet and sound art, and the Tellus Audio Cassette Magazine archive

record.keeps: the work of the artists whose materials it posts, out-of-print or hard-to-procure avant-garde works; it posts some of them without permission and removes a work when its artist asks
record.name: not recorded: the saved sources show no author page and no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names
record.holder: UbuWeb holds copies only; 'The copyrights belong to the copyright holders, not us'; nothing is for sale, the site is commercial-free and volunteer-run, hosted on server space and bandwidth given by universities and partners with no input on content; permanently archived by the Library of Congress
record.function: not recorded for the works beyond the maker's standing: editors select and post works, rights stay with 'the copyright holders', and the artist's one recorded act is the request for removal

lifecycle.detail: founded November 1996; Wikipedia (third party) reports that in January 2024 UbuWeb announced it was no longer active, with the archive preserved in its entirety, and that in February 2025 it resumed its activities; the home page read 2026-11-01 states no status

ubuweb.ls_reading: The archive reads UbuWeb as infrastructure that keeps out-of-print avant-garde work circulating by holding copies while leaving rights with their holders and standing with the artist, whose recorded act is the request for removal. How it names a maker, and so what a collapse of names would lose there, is not shown in the saved sources; its author and work records are unread.

founded.q: UbuWeb was founded in November of 1996, initially as a repository for visual, concrete and, later, sound poetry. Over the years, UbuWeb has embraced all forms of the avant-garde and beyond.

volunteer.q: UbuWeb has no need for funding. All work is done solely on a volunteer basis. Our only cost is our monthly hosting fee, which amounts to US$50 each month.

copyright.q: The copyrights belong to the copyright holders, not us. You'll need to seek them out for proper permission.

not_for_sale.q: Nothing is for sale on UbuWeb. It's all free.

policy.q: If it's out of print, we feel it's fair game. Or if something is in print, yet absurdly priced or insanely hard to procure, we'll take a chance on it. But if it's in print and available to all, we won't touch it.

distribution.q: UbuWeb functions as a distribution center for hard-to-find, out-of-print and obscure materials, transferred digitally to the web.

removal.q: Should something return to print, we will remove it from our site immediately. Also, should an artist find their material posted on UbuWeb without permission and wants it removed, please let us know.

permission.q: Let's face it, if we had to get permission from everyone on UbuWeb, there would be no UbuWeb.

quality.q: We like poor quality because we believe that an institution or an individual wishing to have the "real" thing should purchase it from those who publish and distribute such materials.

fan_copies.q: the crappy, say, VHS rips floating around file-sharing site -- where we get much of our material from -- is gorgeously primitive, made by fans.

independent.q: No. UbuWeb is a completely independent site. However, several universities and partners have generously offered us server space and bandwith, with no restrictions or input regarding our content.

languages.q: Most of our pages are in English; several of them are not.

editors.q: Our editors are pretty much spread across the United States: New York City, Utah, California, etc.

email.q: Due to the volume of email we receive, we unfortunately cannot respond to them all.

commercial_free.q: UbuWeb is completely commercial-free and it will always stay that way.

archive_not_blog.q: UbuWeb is an archive, not a blog.

system.q: coded by hand in BBEdit, all html 1.0. There's no fancy database or back-end.

pennsound.ls_reading: The archive reads PennSound as a witness of a distinct type: a recording keeps the author's name, the performer's voice and a co-composer's credit as separate attributions, so a reading of one poet's work by another collapses into neither. Its filing rule is the poet's name; whether a chosen name is kept as given is not shown beyond the names it files under.

self_description.q: Founded in 1979, the International Dada Archive is a scholarly resource for the study of the historic Dada movement. The Archive has compiled a comprehensive collection of documentation and scholarship relating to Dada.

collection.q: The collection of the International Dada Archive is made up of works by and about the dadaists including books, articles, microfilmed manuscript collections, videorecordings, sound recordings, and online resources.

count.q: Primary access to the entire collection is through the International Online Bibliography of Dada, a catalog containing approximately 60,000 titles.

housed.q: This collection is housed in various departments of the University of Iowa Libraries; most of its holdings are in either the Main Library or the Art Library.

digital_library.q: These books, pamphlets, and periodicals are housed in the Special Collections Department of the University of Iowa Libraries and include many of the major periodicals of the Dada movement from Zurich, Berlin, Paris, and elsewhere, as well as books, exhibition catalogs, and broadsides by participants in the Dada movement.

finding_aids.q: The Archive has also microfilmed a number of public and private manuscript collections containing material on the Dada movement and on individual dadaists. Detailed finding aids exist for each of these microfilmed collections.

curator_away.q: access to some of the Archive's resources is limited when the curator is away.

scanned_entire.q: Each original document has been scanned in its entirety. These are page-image files only, not searchable full-text files.

incomplete_runs.q: In many cases, these are not complete runs of the periodicals.

reprints.q: In a few cases, for the sake of completeness, we have included reprints of issues for which we do not own originals; in those cases, we have omitted any copyrighted materials such as new prefaces and critical annotations.

research_only.q: These documents are provided for research purposes only.

The archive reads it as the legal register of #940's civil-name regime (copyright attaching to legal names) and as the boundary where machine participation is attributed by subtraction: the machine's part is disclaimed and the human remainder is registered as the work's authorship.

authors-guild-human-authored.ls_reading: The archive reads the certificate as an explicit counterposition that asserts authorship's boundary at the human writing of a text, admits machine participation only as 'minimal uses', and binds the non-member's claim to an identity check. It answers #1722's verdict of fakeness for a work with the author's own certification; where machine participation is constitutive of the work, its definition leaves no certifiable place, and the saved page does not say whether the certificate carries the name the author chose.

self_description.q: Human Authored is a project of the Authors Guild that allows an author to certify that their book is created by a human.

definition.q: “Human Authored” means that the text of the book was written by a human and not generated by AI, with the exception of minimal uses such as AI applications that check spelling and grammar or for research.

coverage.q: Human Authored certification is available to all authors with books published in the United States who agree to the licensing terms.

membership.q: Membership is not required but the $10/title fee and identity verification requirement are waived for Authors Guild members.
